title: George Russell luck-adjusted F1 season reveals Kimi Antonelli F1 title truth
excerpt:
George Russell's 2026 F1 season quickly turned into a nightmare as team-mate Kimi Antonelli steamrolled him on his way to winning the title.

Antonelli took the title in round 19 of the season in Mexico City, a result Mercedes boss Toto Wolff described as leaving Russell "distraught", having entered the season as the overwhelming favourite to land the crown.

Russell underlined this status by claiming victory from pole position in Australia, although it came after an early ding-dong battle with the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.

But the season quickly got away from Russell, who has been open and vocal about his struggles with adapting his driving style to the new power units.

The new units, of which 50% of the power output comes from the battery systems require a different driving style, whereby constantly demanding full throttle drains the batteries and leaves the car effectively 50% down on power on straights.

Russell's driving style has always depended on early throttle application on corner exit, something which harms him on straights.

However, the Briton has also suffered more than his fair share of bad luck in 2026.

Therefore, RacingNews365 has had a look at every F1 grand prix between the season-opener in Australia and when Antonelli took the title in Mexico City. We have luck adjusted the the results, i.e given Russell back the result he likely would have achieved, and deducted the points as appropriate from Antonelli's total.

It gives an interesting result...

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

The early races

Round 1 - Australia

Russell - P1 - 25 points

Antonelli - P2 - 18 points

No changes required.

Round 2 - China

Russell, having dominated the weekend in Shanghai through practice and the Sprint, suffered a sudden car issue in Q3 after it ground to a halt, with it turning out he had pulled a padel half a second too soon. Given his strength in the first half of the weekend, it is likely he would have gone on to take pole with a clear run, and probably have converted that into a win. His Sprint win remains unchanged.

Russell - P1 - 58 points. 51 points in reality.

Antonelli - P2 - 40 points. 47 points in reality

Russell earns seven more points; Antonelli loses seven points.

Round 3 - Japan

Russell made a pitstop just prior to the safety car being deployed, clearing the path for a free-stop for Antonelli who went onto win. It is unlikely Russell would have won, given the pace of Antonelli, but given he finished just two seconds behind Oscar Piastri in second, an extra six points is fair.

Russell P2 - 76 points. 63 in reality.

Antonelli P1 - 65 points. 72 points in reality.

Russell earns six more points for a second place finish instead of fourth. Antonelli doesn't change.

Round 4 - Miami

Russell was comprehensively outperformed. No changes to the results or standings needed for either Sprint or grand prix.

Russell P4 - 93 points. 80 in reality.

Antonelli P1 - 100 points. No change from reality.

No changes required.

Round 5 - Canada

Russell was leading when he suffered an engine failure after the duel with Antonelli. It is more than fair to assume he would have gone on to add to his Sprint victory on Saturday.

Russell P1 - 126 points. 88 in reality.

Antonelli P2 - 124 points. 131 in reality.

Russell earns 25 more points for getting the win back, and Antonelli loses seven for dropping from first to second. Sprint remains unchanged.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

The Monaco debacle

Round 6 - Monaco

Antonelli dominated the race with a grand chelem, but Russell was handed a drive-through penalty for not serving a five-second penalty for speeding in the pit-lane at a pit-stop. However, it was found the official timekeepers had incorrectly measured the pit-lane distance, leading to the spate of penalties.

Russell dropped from third on the restart after the red flag to 12th in the final results. In this alternate world, he will receive third place and 15 points back.

Russell P3 - 141 points. In reality, 88 points.

Antonelli P1 - 149 points. In reality, 156 points.

Russell earns 15 points for finishing third. Antonelli's result remains unaffected.

Round 7 - Barcelona

Here, in the interests of fairness, Antonelli's late engine failure must be credited back to him and points deducted from Russell. Antonelli had passed the Briton to run in second place, with Russell third, before Russell took second in the end.

Russell P3 - 156 points. In reality, 106 points.

Antonelli P2 - 167 points. In reality, 156 points.

Antonelli earns his 18 points back for finishing second, and Russell loses three points for falling to third.

Round 8 - Austria

No changes required, as Russell won and Antonelli finished third after a messy afternoon.

Russell P1 - 181 points. In reality, 131 points.

Antonelli P3 - 182 points. In reality, 171 points.

No changes required.

Round 9 - Britain

For the second time, points are added to Antonelli and deducted from Russell - with the Italian set to win the race before a wheelshield failure wrecked the handling of the car and caused him to exceed track limits and earn a time penalty, which was then compounded by the race finishing behind the safety car as he took 15th officially with Russell second. Sprint is unchanged.

Russell P3 - 186 points. In reality, 154 points.

Antonelli P1 - 207 points. In reality, 179 points.

Antonelli earns back 25 points for his lost win, whilst Russell accordingly falls from 18 points for second to third, worth 15 points. No changes to the Sprint.

Round 10 - Belgium

As Antonelli eased to a win, Russell suffered a loss of deployment out of La Source, and was swamped on the run to Les Combes - where he collided with Lewis Hamilton and was out of the race. The deployment issues also likely cost him a front-row in qualifying, as it was worth around two-tenths, and he was 0.191s behind Max Verstappen in second. As such, Russell will be credited with second place instead of a DNF.

Russell P2 - 204 points. In reality, 154 points.

Antonelli P1 - 232 points. In reality, 204 points.

Russell gains 18 points for second place, which he probably should have taken on the grid. Antonelli's win leaves him untouched.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

Russell earns points back

Round 11 - Hungary

In qualifying in Budapest, Russell damaged the sump in his engine in Q3, as he could only manage sixth on the grid - promoted one place due to Antonelli's penalty for ignoring yellow flags. This would have engine penalty consequences later in the season, and he then bogged down off the line due to another glitch. He took seventh in the race as Antonelli was third.

Here, he'll be credited with fourth, given the pace of Lando Norris, Verstappen, and Antonelli in the race.

Russell P4 - 216 points. In reality, 160 points.

Antonelli P3 - 247 points. In reality, 219 points.

Russell earns six more points for finishing fourth, as opposed to the six he took for seventh in real life. Antonelli's haul of 15 for third remain unchanged.

Round 12 - Netherlands

No result change needed as Antonelli was firmly second best and Russell third best, although he did let Antonelli through after a team order request. Russell's Sprint win remains unchanged, where Antonelli was fourth, earning five points.

Russell P3 - 239 points. In reality, 183 points.

Antonelli P2 - 270 points. In reality, 242 points.

No changes required.

Round 13 - Italy

Strictly speaking, Russell should have won the race after starting from pole with Antonelli down in 19th, but he didn't, as Antonelli roared to a famous first home win at Monza since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966. Therefore, as Russell's only problem was that he wasn't fast enough and the other guy was, he doesn't earn anything back.

Russell P2 - 257 points. In reality, 201 points.

Antonelli P1 - 295 points. In reality, 267 points.

No changes required.

Round 14 - Spain

Antonelli was fortunate to earn a victory as Norris lost out due to an unluckily timed safety car. Therefore, Antonelli will drop to second place and lose seven points, whilst Russell fifth place remains unchanged.

Russell P6 - 265 points. In reality, 211 points.

Antonelli P2 - 313 points. In reality, 292 points.

Antonelli loses seven points for dropping to second with Norris winning. Russell's 10 points is unchanged.

Round 15 - Azerbaijan

Russell dominated the weekend, only failing to lead FP3 as he topped every other session and recorded a grand chelem in the race. Antonelli was fifth after climbing from 16th following hitting a wall in Q1, but that is his fault, so receives no credit.

Russell P1 - 290 points. In reality, 226 points.

Antonelli P5 - 323 points. In reality, 302 points.

No changes required.

[Article continues below]

© XPBimages

The closing stages

Round 16 - Bahrain in Malaysia

Russell was running third in the closing laps before the engine failure, which put him out, as Antonelli was second. Therefore, Russell earns 15 points back.

Russell P3 - 305 points. In reality, 236 points.

Antonelli P2 - 341 points. In reality, 320 points.

Russell earns 15 points back for finishing third, as Antonelli's result is unchanged.

Round 17 - Singapore

Russell crashed out of the lead in the Sprint in the wet conditions, an event he likely would have won, but that is driver error and not bad luck, so no points back there.

In the race, he earns four more points, with seventh place possible had he been able to pit during his recovery drive for an engine penalty, with the virtual safety car deployed just as he passed pit-entry and then withdrawn just as he entered the pits. Antonelli unchanged.

Russell P7 - 312 points. In reality, 238 points.

Antonelli P3 - 356 points. In reality, 340 points.

Round 18 - United States

No changes here as Antonelli was dominant from pole and Russell laboured to ninth.

Russell - P9 - 322 points. In reality, 240 points.

Antonelli P1 - 381 points. In reality, 365 points.

No changes required.

Round 19 - Mexico City

Russell qualified second, but suffered a deployment issue on the long run to Turn 1, which dropped him into the pack, for which Wolff apologised. He then picked up a 10-second time penalty for clattering into Hadjar.

He went onto finish in sixth for eight points, but will earn 10 points back for finishing second and taking 18 - but the penalty won't be withdrawn as that was his fault. Antonelli drops from third to fourth, accordingly, and loses three points.

Russell P2 - 340 points. In reality, 250 points.

Antonelli P4 - 393 points. In reality, 380 points.

Russell earns 10 more points for finishing second, whilst Antonelli drops from third to fourth, and loses three.

Round 20 - Sao Paulo

Russell spun in the pit-lane coming out on slicks after the early change from intermediates, but that is driver error, as is the spin from the lead by Antonelli on the next lap. No points back for either.

Russell P4 - 352 points. In reality, 262 points.

Antonelli P5 - 403 points. In reality, 390 points.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

The conclusion

After the exercise, following the Sao Paulo GP, Russell would have 352 points instead of the 262 currently to his name.

This is a loss of 90 points.

For Antonelli, he would hold 403 points, a rise of 13 over his real-life tally of 390 - and crucially, a 51-point lead over Russell.

It would mean that Antonelli could seal the title in the upcoming Las Vegas Grand Prix, where a lead of at least 50 points would suffice - meaning Russell would have to finish at least eighth or better to prolong the fight to Qatar.

© XPB Images

title: Lando Norris shares 'biggest lesson' from failed McLaren F1 title defence
excerpt:
Lando Norris has shared what he believes to be the "biggest lesson" from McLaren's failed title defence in 2026.

Norris was succeeded as world champion by Kimi Antonelli, with McLaren giving up its constructors' title to Mercedes in the first year of the new technical regulations.

Although the Briton has able to take wins in Hungary, the Netherlands and Sao Paulo, and be denied a clear victory in Spain due to an unluckily timed virtual safety car, McLaren has been vying for at least third best all-season with Red Bull, with Mercedes and Ferrari a step ahead.

The reason for this was the fact that both McLaren and Red Bull continued their development of their 2025 cars to ensure they won the titles, whereas Mercedes and Ferrari were able to abandon the projects earlier in favour of the radical new regulations for 2026.

Reflecting, Norris explained how the "biggest lesson" learned was that "nothing comes easy" and that success does not immediately breed even more success.

"The biggest lesson is that nothing comes easy. That’s really it," Norris told media, including RacingNews365.

"Certainly this season, we’ve seen an upgrade battle; we’ve seen better and more consistent performance from our rival teams, and the top two teams, and we’ve seen them performing at a better level than ever before.

"If you look at it this way, a championship doesn’t mean anything for the future. It doesn’t mean you’re going to be more successful; it doesn’t mean anything.

"Every year is a complete reset, and the amount of effort, time and dedication every single person has to put in is harder than the year before.

"Nothing ever comes easy, and you have to always keep working harder than you realise.

"But I certainly don’t want to come across like it has been a negative season."

[Article continues below]

Norris defends McLaren's season

Despite McLaren giving up its two titles to Mercedes, Norris insisted that 2026 was still a successful season for the Woking squad.

"Everyone has high expectations, and so do we," he added.

"We certainly wanted to do better, but in a time where people are doing such a good job as your competition, in a season where the regulation change was so huge, I think you still have to see the season as a successful upturn in events and results more than a disappointment because of how the last two seasons went."

title: Kimi Antonelli names best F1 victory after whirlwind title success
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has selected his historic victory at the Italian Grand Prix as the best of the nine wins which sealed the 2026 drivers' title.

Antonelli claimed the crown with third place in Mexico City to become the youngest F1 champion at 20 years, 2 months, 7 days, following nine wins in the 19 races it took to win the title.

He took five wins on the trot between the Chinese and Monaco Grands Prix, including a grand chelem in the Principality, but it was his seventh win of the season at Monza, Antonelli pinpointed as his best.

In front of his home crowd, Antonelli started from 19th following a back-of-the-grid engine-change penalty, but stormed through the field to defeat team-mate George Russell and take a commanding victory in front of the Tifosi.

Antonelli became the first Italian in 60 years to win at Monza, since Ludovico Scarfiotti won the 1966 race for Ferrari on his way to becoming the heir to Alberto Ascari, who had taken the country's last drivers' title in 1953.

Reflecting, Antonelli named his Monza triumph as his best win, although he also singled out the Belgian Grand Prix - 12 months on from his nadir at Spa, and being left visibly emotional following a difficult weekend.

"It is difficult to say," Antonelli told media, including RacingNews365, when asked which victory was his best.

"I think the best one is yet to come, as always. But if I had to pick one, I would say my home race; it was a very, very special one.

"Then, of course, the first race. The first one is always very, very special, and I think all of them have been very special and very unique in their own ways.

"I think I rate Spa as being a very special one because Spa was probably last year my toughest moment in my career, and coming to this year and winning at a track where I was probably at my lowest, that was very special.

"So, I think all of them have been very special, and hopefully a more special one is coming on its way.

[Article continues below]

Antonelli's damage limitation

When then asked to name the biggest moment of the season, Antonelli pinpointed his consistency, with just one performance-related finish off the podium before winning the title, coming through a fifth-place finish in Azerbaijan after breaking his suspension by hitting a wall in Q1 in qualifying.

"I think it's really hard to pick one. I think the main thing was the consistency we've had during the whole season because even when it was looking a bit rough, we still managed to do a decent result, managed to do some damage limitation," he said.

"That has been the key, always been there. And also, I think enjoying every weekend, enjoying the weekends, facing the weekend and going to the weekend with passion and love for the sport, for what I do, and just trying as well to appreciate every moment.

"[Mexico City] was very difficult emotionally as well. It hasn't been easy, but I still tried to appreciate the day, coming to the track having that feeling that it could have been the day, and also the feeling on the grid.

"I've been really trying to enjoy every moment, and that has been the thing of the season for me with the team. Just taking it race by race and enjoying the weekend on and off the track, enjoying the time with the mechanics, with the engineers and with everyone involved, because at the end, I've still got to remember that I'm very lucky to do what I love to do as a profession."

title: Christian Horner reveals major unhappiness during Max Verstappen dominance
excerpt:
Christian Horner has revealed that he was privately unhappy during Red Bull's period of utter dominance with Max Verstappen, despite the team sweeping all before it on track.

The former Red Bull team principal, who left the Milton Keynes-based squad in July 2025 after 20 years at the helm, opened up on the High Performance podcast about the toll the job took on him even as results flowed in his favour.

Horner was dismissed by Red Bull following a stretch of internal discord and leadership upheaval, with his exit formalised in a settlement reached in September 2025.

But he has now gone public with how he really felt behind the scenes during the team's most successful years with Verstappen.

Asked why he felt relief at leaving Red Bull, Horner explained that the atmosphere around the team had shifted dramatically from when he first joined.

"I think, obviously, tension had grown, things had changed, and it just felt very, very different from when I came into the sport, into the team," Horner said.

"And when I got in the car, and I left that meeting, I called Geri, my wife, explained what happened, and you just feel like the world's been almost taken off your shoulders."

"Incredibly sad, and as I drove back up the M40 home, I had a chance to reflect a little. But, if I'm really honest with myself, and if you spoke to my wife, there was a period in time when we were winning a huge amount, and she said, 'I've never seen you so unhappy.'

"It's almost like you get to the top of the mountain, and you realise there's nothing there.

"It was that kind of feeling, and obviously a huge amount of pressure in a sport that is so visible as well."

[Article continues below]

Christian Horner explains what caused unhappiness emotions

The period Horner refers to coincides with Red Bull's dominant 2023 campaign, when internal factions reportedly formed within the team following the October 2022 death of co-founder Dietrich Mateschitz.

That power vacuum is said to have fuelled friction between different camps at Red Bull, even as the team swept to results on track.

Pressed on how he could feel so negative during such a triumphant stretch for the team, Horner pointed directly to the death of Mateschitz as the turning point.

"I think it's all relative, and it applies across so many different aspects of life," he said. "That if you're happy in yourself, if you're happy in your work, then everything's just easier."

"And there's been an awful lot of change, obviously within the team, within the overall business, and then different pressures are settling down as to what does the new world after the passing of the founder, Dietrich Mateschitz, look like?

"And inevitably, it was always going to be different from that moment onwards. And rather than being able to focus on just the racing, suddenly your energy, your focus gets consumed into managing other elements and other relationships and politics, which inevitably happen within many different organisations."

title: Lewis Hamilton 'message to Italy' theory raised after public Charles Leclerc fallout
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton was left furious with Ferrari in Mexico City, but were his comments really aimed at Maranello?

Martin Brundle believes Lewis Hamilton's furious reaction to Ferrari's handling of the Mexico City Grand Prix was aimed squarely at the team's Italian hierarchy.

Hamilton finished second behind Max Verstappen after Charles Leclerc's attempt to pass him around the outside of Turn 4 sent both Ferrari drivers off the circuit, with Leclerc rejoining in the lead.

The stewards handed Leclerc a reduced five-second penalty, having accounted for the fact Hamilton also ran wide, but the incident ultimately cost Ferrari a likely one-two and instead handed the win to Verstappen.

Post-race, Hamilton claimed he was "really pi**ed" at having lost a one-two finish and claimed that Leclerc had a "do or die attitude" and raced him differently compared to other drivers, as boss Fred Vasseur claimed that the pair had shown Ferrari a "lack of respect."

Clear-the-air talks were then held in Brazil, but speaking to Sky F1, Brundle said Hamilton's anger on the radio reflected a driver who no longer feels the need to hold back.

"He's at the stage of his career and his life where he's going to be unfiltered, and he was pretty unhappy with what happened," Brundle said.

"He said on the radio that they've given Charles the win today with just that five-second penalty, and it's definitely worth cutting a few corners, getting out front. You make a lot more than five seconds.

"But the big story is it didn't give a Ferrari driver the win at all. It gave Max Verstappen the victory as it happened. It wasn't the smartest move in Charles's career and life. Trying to go around the outside of Turn 4, that was a 75-25 against move against your teammate. It just wasn't a smart move.

"Lewis has realised, here's a chance to actually make a bit of ground on this, because that was a bit silly."

[Article continues below]

Lewis Hamilton eyes increased Ferrari 'clout'

Brundle went on to frame the episode as part of a wider shift in how modern F1 teams expect their drivers to behave, pointing to the sheer scale of today's organisations compared to the sport he grew up in.

"But, you know, I was thinking about this in the week," Brundle continued. "When I first was in Formula 1, I think we had 40 people in the team. Now there are 2,000 people in the team.

"You've got this situation where they say you're representing 2,000 people, and it's true. But you're in Formula 1. As an individual sports person, you're measured as an individual sports person in a team environment. Now that team's 2,000 people, and it's almost becoming impossible.

"I think we saw the same with Lando [Norris] and Oscar [Piastri]. Where do you stand as a driver. I think this is a new challenge, on where do I really stand here.

"You can't just keep criticising me for racing for myself just because I'm in a team. It actually doesn't work, does it, if you think about it."

Brundle also drew a parallel with Hamilton's combustible spell alongside Nico Rosberg at Mercedes, suggesting friction of this kind was always likely to resurface once Hamilton found himself fighting a teammate for position again.

"I seem to remember him and Nico [Rosberg] running into each other quite dramatically on a few occasions, having quite a spat. It's inevitable," Brundle insisted.

"I stand by what I said. I think Lewis has realised there's a really good platform to carve himself out more of a number one spot there, more clout in that situation. He's not going to let that go.

"And that comment, when he got out of the car during the red flag, of, 'We've got big problems here, big problems,' that wasn't to anybody around in Mexico. That was to some people in Italy."

title: Oscar Piastri dismisses F1 title collapse link to ongoing McLaren woes
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri does not believe his collapse in the 2025 F1 title race is linked to his ongoing struggles in the 2026 season.

Following his last victory to date in the 2025 Dutch Grand Prix, Piastri held a 34-point lead over team-mate Lando Norris and a 104-point advantage over Max Verstappen, with seven rounds remaining.

However, a crash in qualifying in Azerbaijan was the start of a poor run of form, with the Australian jumping the start in Baku before crashing on the opening lap, before expressing fury in Singapore after being barged past by Norris at Turn 2 on the first lap.

Then, in the United States, Piastri was generally held responsible for triggering a first-corner shunt in the Sprint that also eliminated Norris, before crashing out of the Sao Paulo Sprint.

In the Singapore-United States-Mexico City-Sao Paulo leg, Piastri finished fourth once and fifth three times, as Norris and Verstappen hit top form, with Piastri's fifth in Mexico coming as Norris won to climb to the top of the standings.

Piastri and Norris were then disqualified in Las Vegas for plank wear, with McLaren's strategy faux pas in Qatar then meaning an easy win became second to Verstappen as Norris ultimately won the title on 423 points, with Verstappen in second on 421 and Piastri third on 410, having led the table for 15 of the 24 rounds after a fast start, which included five wins in the first nine races.

In 2026, Piastri has claimed just two podium finishes all season, and has not finished in the top three since the Miami Grand Prix, with an average finishing place of 7.1 in the 16 races since, with Norris claiming three victories in a difficult MCL40 machine.

McLaren boss Andrea Stella has put Piastri's struggles down to his inability to adapt quickly to the new way the 2026 cars must be driven, with lack of downforce meaning the cars are subject to constant micro-corrections, something opposed to Piastri's uber-smooth driving style.

Reflecting on a tough season, Piastri explained that as far as he was concerned, his 2025 collapse has had no impact on his 2026 woes - and that he is "under no illusions" at the scale of the challenge in recapturing his best form.

"I'll be using the off-season to have a bit of a reset, have a bit of a rethink, and [having] a clear start is going to be useful," Piastri told the Up to Speed podcast.

"I don't think these problems are going to solve themselves in an off-season without putting a lot of effort into it, so there's definitely going to be a lot of hard work involved.

"The cars will evolve. The regulations are changing a little bit again next year, and we have to see what kind of tyres we have next year, because that can also make a difference.

"I'm under no illusion that it's magically going to be different next year. But I think, honestly, in some ways, last year going the way it did, I think if it had gone better last year, it would have made this year even more painful.

"I think a lot of the struggles this year, or all the struggles this year, are unrelated to what happened last year. It's been a separate issue, and this year has definitely taught me a lot. I feel like I'm getting on top of some of these struggles.

"Maybe not as consistently as I would like at the moment, but I think even Brazil qualifying didn't go to plan. But actually, the pace I had in the race was the strongest I've had for a long time. So, there are definitely signs of positives there.

"It is definitely one of those things where I'm going to have to go and grab it and pull things in the direction I want rather than hoping things come to me naturally."

Piastri continues on title collapse

When then asked why his title challenge had unravelled towards the end of the season, Piastri indicated he would do certain things "differently."

"[It was] for a number of reasons, really," he began.

"I think there were a couple of places where I just struggled for pace, and I think again some of those specifics are also present this year. I think also as a team we would definitely do some things a bit differently if we did it again.

"The impact of some of those things was big sometimes. And again, I think as a team we know what we would do differently if we were in that position this year.

"We've not had to worry about that because that's not the position we've been in. But I think some things would be done differently."
